Q: Android Studio Emulator keeps exiting with error 139 on ubuntu 24.04 A:

There are two physical GPU, while it is unclear which -gpu option is being passed.

emuglConfig_init: vulkan_mode_selected:host gles_mode_selected:host

emuglConfig_get_vulkan_hardware_gpu_support_info: Found physical GPU 'NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2070 with Max-Q Design', type: VK_PHYSICAL_DEVICE_TYPE_DISCRETE_GPU, apiVersion: 1.4.325, driverVersion: 590.48
emuglConfig_get_vulkan_hardware_gpu_support_info: Found physical GPU 'Intel(R) UHD Graphics (CML GT2)', type: VK_PHYSICAL_DEVICE_TYPE_INTEGRATED_GPU, apiVersion: 1.4.318, driverVersion: 25.2.8

The command line is the first line ...

emulator -netdelay none -netspeed full -avd Medium_Phone_API_36.1 -qt-hide-window -grpc-use-token -idle-grpc-timeout 300

To debug, add options -gpu, -verbose. Or try to disable Vulkan -feature -Vulkan.
There's no way to tell which GPU to use. One GPU being present is being assumed.

I don't know what "UHD Graphics (CML GT2)" means, but the UHD 620 has known issues with Vulkan: Emulator Not Starting-up in Android Studio: The emulator process for AVD has terminated

Intel's Comet Lake GT2 GPU is probably something alike UHD 630.

Just see Troubleshoot known issues with Android Emulator

  • If your machine has both an Intel GPU and a discrete GPU, disable the Intel GPU in Device Manager to ensure you are using the discrete GPU.

Q: How do I specify three different types of response in the Go application using usecase.Interactor A:

The fundamental issue is that Go's type system and swaggo/swag-style libraries don't map cleanly onto oneOf — Go generics with union constraints exist only for compile-time type checking, not runtime polymorphism. You have two practical options with standard Go.

Option 1: Use any as the response type, document oneOf manually

The simplest fix within your current setup — return any at runtime and accept that the auto-doc won't infer the oneOf automatically:

func getInfoIn1C(tel string) (any, error) {
    // return one of ResponsePhoneExist, ResponsePhoneNoExist, ResponsePhoneInArchive
}

You'd then manually annotate or extend the generated spec to add the oneOf. Not ideal since you lose the "auto" in auto-documentation.

Option 2: Use a discriminated wrapper struct

Make a single response type that contains optional fields from all variants, using omitempty:

type ResponsePhone struct {
    Result      string `json:"result"`
    Info        string `json:"info"`        // "ok", "no exist", "archive"
    Phonenumber string `json:"phonenumber"`
    Count       int    `json:"count,omitempty"`
    Activated   string `json:"activated,omitempty"`
}

This is honest about what the wire format actually looks like (one JSON object with some fields sometimes absent), and auto-doc tools can describe it correctly. The oneOf in your spec is a documentation convenience — the actual responses are already a subset of a single shape.

If you're open to a different framework, Rivaas handles oneOf directly through WithResponse — you pass each possible response type and the generated spec will reflect it:

a.POST("/phonenumber/get",
    getPhoneInfoHandler,
    app.WithDoc(
        openapi.WithRequest(RequestInfo{}),
        openapi.WithResponse(200, ResponsePhoneExist{}),
        openapi.WithResponse(200, ResponsePhoneNoExist{}),
        openapi.WithResponse(200, ResponsePhoneInArchive{}),
    ),
)

Multiple WithResponse calls for the same status code generate a oneOf in the spec. Your handler still returns any at runtime — but the documentation correctly describes all three shapes without any manual YAML or annotation tricks.

Disclosure: I'm the author of Rivaas.

Q: How to test a function in Visual Studio 2010? A:

That's what unit tests are for. The other option is simply create a new console test to reference it, however simply right clicking on it and creating a new unit test is easy, and the best method - it is not overkill and takes 5 seconds :)

Worst case, just delete your test when it's done.

Q: Aggregating multiple columns in polars with missing or nan values A:

I think existing answers address your questions nicely

Just want to add that if you want to have more generic option of adding multiple aggregates, you can use syntactic sugar versions of aggregates and make it extendable:

# list of tuples (aggregate, suffix)
aggregates = [(pl.sum, '_sum'), (pl.median, '_median')]

(
    data
    .group_by('x')
    .agg(
        f_agg("*").name.suffix(f_suf) for f_agg, f_suf in aggregates
    )
)

┌─────┬───────┬───────┬───────┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────┐
│ x   ┆ y_sum ┆ z_sum ┆ m_sum ┆ y_median ┆ z_median ┆ m_median │
│ --- ┆ ---   ┆ ---   ┆ ---   ┆ ---      ┆ ---      ┆ ---      │
│ str ┆ i64   ┆ f64   ┆ f64   ┆ f64      ┆ f64      ┆ f64      │
╞═════╪═══════╪═══════╪═══════╪══════════╪══════════╪══════════╡
│ b   ┆ 17    ┆ NaN   ┆ NaN   ┆ 5.0      ┆ 8.0      ┆ 8.0      │
│ a   ┆ 37    ┆ NaN   ┆ NaN   ┆ 6.5      ┆ 2.0      ┆ 3.5      │
└─────┴───────┴───────┴───────┴──────────┴──────────┴──────────┘

Q: Select polars columns by index A:

Example data.

import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({
    "a": [1, 2, 3],
    "b": [True, False, False],
    "c": ["a", "b", "c"],
})

Since polars 0.20.26 there exists pl.nth as idiomatic way to select columns by index.

Using a single index.

df.select(pl.nth(0))

shape: (3, 1)
┌─────┐
│ a   │
│ --- │
│ i64 │
╞═════╡
│ 1   │
│ 2   │
│ 3   │
└─────┘

Using a list of indices (introduced in version 0.20.27).

df.select(pl.nth([0, 2]))

shape: (3, 2)
┌─────┬─────┐
│ a   ┆ c   │
│ --- ┆ --- │
│ i64 ┆ str │
╞═════╪═════╡
│ 1   ┆ a   │
│ 2   ┆ b   │
│ 3   ┆ c   │
└─────┴─────┘

Using a range of indices. (introduced in version 0.20.27).

df.select(pl.nth(range(0, 2)))

shape: (3, 2)
┌─────┬───────┐
│ a   ┆ b     │
│ --- ┆ ---   │
│ i64 ┆ bool  │
╞═════╪═══════╡
│ 1   ┆ true  │
│ 2   ┆ false │
│ 3   ┆ false │
└─────┴───────┘

Q: How to update a polars dataframe column at a specific range? A:

After some testing, the fastest solution by far is to build the new column ourselves, by appending together the old values and the ones we want to update:

start, stop, value = 0, 3, -1

df = df.with_columns(
    foo=data[0 : start, "foo"]
    .append(pl.repeat(value, stop - start, eager=True, dtype=data["foo"].dtype))
    .append(data[stop : len(data), "foo"]),
)

However, it results in a series with 3 chunks, which might make further computations slower. All the other following solutions result in a uniquely chunked series, but are 10x slower.

Using scatter.

df = df.with_columns(df["foo"].scatter(range(start, stop), value))

Using extend instead of append:

df = df.with_columns(
    foo=data[0 : start, "foo"]
    .extend(pl.repeat(value, stop - start, eager=True, dtype=data["foo"].dtype))
    .extend(data[stop : len(data), "foo"]),
)

Using when

df = df.with_row_index().with_columns(
    pl.when(pl.col("index").is_between(start, stop))
    .then(value)
    .otherwise(pl.col("foo")),
)

Using update.

df = df.with_row_index().update(
    pl.select(
        pl.int_range(start, stop, dtype=pl.UInt32).alias("index"),
        pl.lit(value),
    ),
    on="index",
)
